title: COP31: Canada, UK reaffirm $1.3 trillion climate finance goal, announce new commitments
content: Canada and the UK reaffirm their commitment to mobilising at least $1.3 trillion annually in climate finance for developing countries by 2035, as agreed at COP29. Canada outlines a five-year goal of more than C$14 billion in climate-related support, including C$116 million for 12 new projects. The UK announces around £6 billion in international climate finance through development assistance over three years, alongside £6.7 billion in other public investments. Both countries reiterate support for tripling adaptation finance by 2035, even as disagreements over climate funding continue at COP31. Developing countries need an estimated $305 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, while international public adaptation finance stood at just $28.2–31.7 billion in 2024. Canada and the United Kingdom have reaffirmed their commitment to scaling up climate finance for developing countries, outlining funding plans as negotiations over global finance targets continue at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. In a joint statement on November 13 , Canada's Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Nature Julie Dabrusin and UK Minister of State for Climate Transition Katie White reiterated their support for the New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG), agreed at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024. The agreement calls for climate finance for developing countries to reach at least $1.3 trillion annually by 2035 from all sources, with developed countries taking the lead in mobilising at least $300 billion annually. Both ministers reaffirmed their countries' obligations under Article 9 of the Paris Agreement to provide financial resources to developing countries. They also supported efforts to triple adaptation finance by 2035, following discussions at COP30 in Belém, Brazil.

title: COP31: Over 100 major polluter groups represented at climate summit, outnumber delegates from vulnerable nations
content: More than 100 major polluter corporations and industry associations are represented at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, according to a civil society analysis. Delegates linked to these groups outnumber those from several climate-vulnerable nations, including Nepal, Niger and the Philippines. Representatives from 30 major banks attended the summit; together, these banks provided more than $2.2 trillion in fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025. Campaigners warn that organisations with records of opposing stronger climate policies could undermine negotiations, while an oil industry representative defends their participation. A separate Transparency International analysis found that 19% of participants on national delegations had not disclosed their relationship with those delegations. More than 100 corporations and industry associations linked to major polluting sectors have representatives at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP 31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in Antalya, Türkiye, raising concerns about their potential influence over negotiations, according to two analyses released on November 13, 2026. The reports, published by the Kick Big Polluters Out (KBPO) coalition and Transparency International, raise questions about industry access to climate negotiations and the transparency of national delegations. The KBPO analysis also found that banks represented at the summit had collectively provided more than $2.2 trillion in fossil fuel financing between 2021 and 2025. Civil society groups argue that companies with records of opposing climate policies should not be given disproportionate access to negotiations intended to address the climate crisis. Big Polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma, and survival challenges for our people. We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations Prakash Dalal of Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal
